questions.q: On the 5-node graph from Chapter 1's lab, what fraction of the 32 possible starting points caused greedy local search to get stuck below the true optimum of 5?
questions.explain: Direct computation across all 32 starting points showed 24 reached the true optimum of 5, while 8 (25%) got stuck at a local optimum of only 4 -- a concrete demonstration that greedy search is not reliable even on a small graph.

questions.q: What single mechanism allows simulated annealing to escape local optima that trap greedy local search?
options: It sometimes accepts a worsening move, with probability e^(Delta/T), allowing it to move away from a local trap rather than only ever improving
It restarts from a completely random new starting point every single step
It increases the number of nodes in the graph during the search
It always accepts every possible move regardless of whether it improves or worsens the solution
questions.explain: Unlike greedy search, which only ever accepts improving moves, simulated annealing accepts worsening moves with probability e^(Delta/T) -- exactly the mechanism that let it escape the trap at x=(0,1,0,0,0) where greedy got stuck.

questions.q: Starting from the exact same point x=(0,1,0,0,0) where greedy got stuck at cut=4, what result did simulated annealing achieve across 5 different random seeds?
options: All 5 runs also got stuck at cut=4, identical to greedy
All 5 runs reached the true optimum of cut=5
Only 1 of 5 runs reached cut=5; the other 4 stayed at cut=4
All 5 runs produced a worse result than greedy, at cut=3
questions.explain: Running simulated annealing from the identical starting point across 5 different seeds, all 5 runs found the true optimum of 5 -- demonstrating this wasn't a lucky one-off result but a reliable escape from the trap.

questions.q: What does branch-and-bound (used in commercial solvers like CPLEX and Gurobi) guarantee that simulated annealing does not?
options: A random, unpredictable result with no bound on its quality
A faster runtime than any heuristic method on every possible problem instance
The ability to run on quantum hardware without any classical computation
A provably optimal answer when run to completion, or a guaranteed gap to the true optimum if it must stop early
questions.explain: Branch-and-bound systematically partitions and prunes the search space using provable bounds, guaranteeing a provably optimal answer if run to completion, or at minimum a certified gap to the true optimum -- a transparency heuristics like SA generally cannot offer.

questions.q: Why does the lesson insist that quantum optimization results be benchmarked against simulated annealing and branch-and-bound solvers specifically, rather than against brute force or no baseline at all?
options: Because these classical methods represent the realistic competition -- the actual tools industry already uses -- and a quantum result only means something if it's compared fairly against the real alternatives, not a weak strawman
Because simulated annealing always performs worse than brute force, making it an easy benchmark to beat
Because branch-and-bound solvers cannot be run on any classical computer
Because quantum algorithms are mathematically incapable of being compared to brute-force search
questions.explain: Simulated annealing and branch-and-bound solvers are the realistic heuristic and exact-answer competition respectively -- benchmarking a quantum result against them (rather than an unoptimized or nonexistent baseline) is what makes any comparison honest, setting up Lesson 21's fair-benchmark design.
